run: Battery + → master disconnect → Class-T → dash post busbar
cable: 2 AWG fine-strand, loomed, grommeted, pull string beside it in the tunnel
protection: Class-T 150 A at the battery — the PMU stud's maximum
why: Class-T is the only common fuse with the interrupt rating to break a lithium short. The cable between post and fuse is the one length that can never be protected - keep it inches long. The master disconnect is on the POSITIVE and carries this leg and B2 both (D-319, supersedes D-245): one switch that genuinely kills the car, which is what ABYC E-9.10.c and NHRA both expect and what a first responder will look for.

run: Battery + → master disconnect → MRBF → starter B+ stud
protection: MRBF 250 A (D-237 → D-321) on the post
why: Cranking pulls 300–500 A briefly and cannot pass through the 150 A Class-T. 1/0 over 18 ft keeps about half a volt at the starter that 2 AWG would have lost (D-246)

protection: F18 100 A MIDI at the stud
why: The alternator charges through the starter cable, as the factory did through its fusible link

protection: F17 30 A MIDI at the stud
why: The start relay's contact current never touches the PMU; O21 only drives the coil

Straight to the stud - the disconnect is on the positive (D-319, supersedes D-245). The negative leg is never switched: any parallel negative bond (a shunt, a BMS or heater return, a charger left on) would silently become the return path for the whole car. Bare metal, star washer, cavity wax at the stud

run: Rear ground stud → engine block (through the tunnel)
cable: 1/0, loomed, pulled beside the starter feed
why: The dedicated cranking return (D-246). Without it 400 A crosses the whole unibody through 44-year-old spot welds and seam sealer; the factory never asked the shell to do this because the battery was in the engine bay. B6 stays as the block-to-chassis bond, not the main return
The block-to-chassis bond. The cranking return is B7's dedicated 1/0 (D-246); without this strap the current finds its own path through throttle cables and sender wires
